The paper surveys the rapid rise of robotic foundation models (RFMs) as a response to the industrial transition from fixed, high‑speed manipulators to collaborative cobots that must be commissioned quickly, redeployed across variable processes, and operate safely alongside humans. It argues that adaptive low‑level control is now the primary bottleneck and proposes a hierarchical taxonomy that spans from rule‑based systems to generalist models capable of zero‑shot online adaptation. Noting a surge of RFMs around 2025 and a lack of systematic industrial evaluation, the authors construct three literature corpora with a modular Python pipeline that translates queries across arXiv, Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scopus and Semantic Scholar, removes duplicates, enriches missing metadata, and filters relevance using GPT‑4o scoring. The main RFM corpus contains 1 025 highly relevant works, of which 324 focus on manipulation‑oriented, control‑centric RFMs; an industrial‑implication corpus of 125 top‑scored papers supplies eleven domain‑agnostic requirements (adaptability, safety/compliance, reliability, multimodal interaction, real‑time performance, cost‑effective integration, sensor‑fusion, benchmarking, data‑efficient learning, cybersecurity, explainability). These requirements are expanded into 47 detailed attributes, forming an 11 × 47 matrix (517 implication‑attribute cells) that underpins a catalogue of 149 criteria covering model capabilities, ecosystem documentation, and hybrid responsibilities such as hot‑swapping, out‑of‑distribution robustness, calibrated uncertainty, human‑in‑the‑loop clarification, supervisory failure detection, and memory governance.

An automated evaluation pipeline queries GPT‑5.1 for each of the 324 manipulation RFMs against every criterion, returning binary fulfilment judgments, confidence scores, evidence flags and rationales. Validation on three expert‑annotated papers shows 96.6 % accuracy, κ≈0.74, a 1.9 % false‑positive rate and a 22.6 % false‑negative rate, reflecting a conservative policy that marks a criterion unfulfilled unless clearly supported. The resulting maturity scores exhibit a pronounced ceiling effect: the five highest‑rated models achieve only 0.11–0.12 of the total criteria (≈10 %). Gemini Robotics 1.5 attains the best overall score (0.12) and a peak implication score of 0.44; other top models show isolated peaks (e.g., Collab‑VLA I10 = 0.21, GF‑VLA I11 = 0.27). Thus current RFMs address narrow subsets of industrial needs rather than providing uniform, end‑to‑end readiness.

Hardware analysis reveals that typical cobots have six degrees of freedom, median payloads ≈5.5 kg, reaches near 0.9 m, positioning accuracies of 0.05–0.09 mm, and low power consumption (~0.3 kW), contrasting with conventional robots that consume several kilowatts. Edge AI platforms are therefore essential. A comparative study of NVIDIA Jetson devices finds the Orin Nano offers the lowest purchase price with high TOPS‑per‑dollar, the Xavier NX provides the smallest power envelope (15 W), and the Orin AGX 32 GB balances throughput (200 TOPS) and efficiency; high‑end RTX 5090 and Thor series deliver greater compute at substantially higher energy cost, limiting suitability for mobile or battery‑constrained deployments.

Across the full corpus, research emphasis concentrates on adaptability, benchmarking, and data usage, with breadth scores above 0.70 for these implications but depth (average criterion fulfilment) below 0.10 for all. The Top‑50 subset improves breadth to full coverage for several implications yet still shows depth under 0.04 for safety/compliance and real‑time performance. Gap analysis indicates mismatches exceeding 0.8 for most implications, confirming that implementations fall far short of delivering comprehensive, criterion‑complete solutions, especially for safety, real‑time operation, cost‑effectiveness, and human‑robot interaction.

The authors conclude that despite benchmark gains, existing RFMs lack the integrated, reliable, safe, and low‑latency performance demanded by real‑world factories. They call for traceable, industrial‑focused assessment frameworks, tighter multimodal sensing integration, robust uncertainty handling, and hardware‑aware model design, as well as layered architectures that combine planning, memory, verification and safety gating, to bridge the gap between laboratory success and deployable cobot intelligence.
